title: Training logistic regression

sections.title: 10.3 Where the log loss comes from
10.5 Code from scratch, checked against scikit-learn

html:
Purpose. To use logistic regression you must find its weights. That needs a cost function that fits probabilities, then the same gradient descent as before. The surprise is how little changes.

Key ideas

  • Squared error is a bad cost for logistic regression: with a sigmoid it gives a bumpy surface. The right cost is the log loss.
  • The log loss punishes a confident wrong answer very hard.
  • The gradient has exactly the same form as for linear regression: (prediction minus target) times the feature. Only the prediction is now a sigmoid.
  • At w = 0 and b = 0 the cost is always 0.693, the natural log of 2. This is a quick bug check.

10.1 Why not squared error?

If you put the sigmoid inside the squared-error cost, the cost surface is no longer a single bowl: it has flat patches and traps, and gradient descent may get stuck. A different cost keeps the bowl shape (Ng, video 34).

10.2 The loss on one example

For one example with true label y and prediction f (a probability):

  • If y = 1, the loss is -log(f). When f is near 1 the loss is near 0. When f is near 0 the loss explodes.
  • If y = 0, the loss is -log(1 - f). The same, mirrored.
True y Prediction f Loss Reading
1 0.9 0.105 right and confident: a small penalty
1 0.5 0.693 undecided
1 0.1 2.303 wrong and confident: a big penalty
0 0.1 0.105 right and confident
0 0.9 2.303 wrong and confident

The model is encouraged to be right, and to be humble when it is unsure. Because y is either 0 or 1, the two cases fit in one line (Ng, video 35), and the cost J is the average of this loss over all m examples:

J(w⃗,b)=−1m∑i=1m[y(i)log⁡f(x⃗(i))+(1−y(i))log⁡(1−f(x⃗(i)))]J(\vec{w},b) = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left[ y^{(i)} \log f(\vec{x}^{(i)}) + \left(1 - y^{(i)}\right) \log\left(1 - f(\vec{x}^{(i)})\right) \right]

When y is 1 the second term vanishes, and when y is 0 the first does, which gives the two cases above. At w = 0 and b = 0 every prediction is 0.5, so every loss is -log(0.5) = 0.693, and so is the average. If your code does not print 0.693 there, it has a bug.

10.3 Where the log loss comes from

Beyond the videos (StatQuest's Logistic Regression Details Pt 2 shows it step by step). The log loss is maximum likelihood in disguise. The likelihood is the probability that the model assigned to exactly what happened: multiply f for every example with y = 1 and (1 - f) for every example with y = 0. The best parameters make that product as large as possible. A product of many small numbers is awkward, so take the logarithm, which turns it into a sum, and flip the sign so that "largest likelihood" becomes "smallest cost". The result is the cost above. So it is not an arbitrary choice: it is the principle of making the observed data as probable as possible.

10.4 The gradient

wj:=wj−α1m∑i=1m(fw⃗,b(x⃗(i))−y(i))xj(i)b:=b−α1m∑i=1m(fw⃗,b(x⃗(i))−y(i))w_j := w_j - \alpha \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( f_{\vec{w},b}(\vec{x}^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)} \qquad b := b - \alpha \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( f_{\vec{w},b}(\vec{x}^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right)

This looks exactly like the linear regression update from Chapter 7, and Ng points out how surprising that is. The difference is hidden inside f: for linear regression it is w . x + b, and here it is the sigmoid of w . x + b (Ng, video 36). It is not a coincidence: both come from the same family of models (generalized linear models), and the cost was designed that way.

10.5 Code from scratch, checked against scikit-learn

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def cost(w, b, X, y):
    f = sigmoid(X @ w + b)
    return -np.mean(y * np.log(f) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - f))

def fit(X, y, alpha=0.5, steps=5000):
    m, n = X.shape
    w, b = np.zeros(n), 0.0
    for _ in range(steps):
        err = sigmoid(X @ w + b) - y            # prediction minus target
        w = w - alpha * (X.T @ err) / m
        b = b - alpha * err.mean()
    return w, b

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
X = rng.normal(size=(400, 2))                              # two features, already on similar scales
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.7, 400) > 0.5).astype(float)

print(round(cost(np.zeros(2), 0.0, X, y), 3))              # 0.693
w, b = fit(X, y)
print(np.round(w, 3), round(b, 3))                         # [2.617 2.412] -1.063
sk = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, tol=1e-10, max_iter=10000).fit(X, y)   # C=inf means no regularization
print(np.round(sk.coef_[0], 3), np.round(sk.intercept_[0], 3))          # [2.617 2.412] -1.063
pred = sigmoid(X @ w + b) >= 0.5
print(round((pred == y).mean(), 3), round(max(y.mean(), 1 - y.mean()), 3))   # 0.862 0.62  accuracy vs baseline

The handmade model and scikit-learn agree to three decimals. The model gets 86.2% right against a baseline of 62% (always guessing the majority class). That is the comparison to make every time (Chapter 3). Note that this accuracy is on the training data. A fair score needs held-out data.

10.6 In practice

  • Scale the features first (Chapter 8), or gradient descent will crawl.
  • If one class is rare (defaults, fraud), accuracy is a poor yardstick; read Chapter 12.
  • Add regularization when you have many features or little data (Chapter 11).
  • scikit-learn's LogisticRegression has regularization on by default, with strength C, where C is 1 divided by lambda. For an unregularized fit, as above, pass C=np.inf.

Loan example. Train a classifier on the offers table with label Accepted. Hold out 20% of the rows, scale with the training mean and standard deviation, fit your own function and scikit-learn on the same scaled features, and check that the weights agree. Then compare the held-out accuracy with the baseline of predicting the most common outcome. This is exactly the Wednesday drill of week 3.

Common mistakes

  • Using squared error as the cost.
  • Writing log(0): if a prediction is exactly 0 or 1 and wrong, the loss is infinite. Libraries clip the values slightly away from 0 and 1.
  • Reporting training accuracy as if it were the real score.
  • Comparing your weights with scikit-learn's without setting the same regularization.

Check yourself

  • Compute the loss for y = 1 when f = 0.8, and for y = 0 when f = 0.8.
  • Why is the cost exactly 0.693 at w = 0, b = 0?
  • What changes between the gradient for linear and logistic regression?
  • Why does log loss punish a confident wrong answer so hard, and is that desirable?
Show answers

(1) -ln(0.8) = 0.223 and -ln(0.2) = 1.609. (2) Every prediction is 0.5, and -ln(0.5) = 0.693 for either label. (3) Only the prediction f: a sigmoid in the logistic case. (4) The loss grows without limit as a wrong prediction approaches certainty. That is desirable, because it pushes the model to be calibrated: do not claim certainty you do not have.
